newsitem.title: MEXICO: Pemex cleans up, vows greater environmental care.
newsitem.headline: Pemex cleans up, vows greater environmental care.

text.p: Almost one year after a fatal blast ravaged Mexico's most important natural gas processing site, the remodeled Cactus complex features fauna, a shiny facade and even a fish pool.

Couched between miles of lush greenery, banana and cocoa plantations on the border in southern Chiapas state, Cactus drew national attention on July 26 last year when a gas leak led to a late night explosion. Seven people died, scores were injured and production was crippled for months.
But at the inauguration of a renovated plant on Thursday, Cactus showed a different face. The entry to the complex was redone and gleaming as visitors were brought in to tour the site.

Director general of state oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) Adrian Lajous rode through the complex, noting that Cactus had been cleaned up and made environment-friendly in the 10 months since the accident.
Instead of a junkyard with charred bits from the explosion, Pemex planted grass and plants and built a fish pond amid the site's piping and machinery.
Pemex officials apologized in the tour for patches of mud. "We used up all the available sod in the region," they said.
The makeover is part of a push to improve Pemex's security and environmental record.
"Security and environmental protection are values that are equally important as production, transportation, sales, quality and costs," Lajous told reporters.
Pemex has said the gas leak was caused by human error. Two other accidents since then have also resulted in fatalities, drawing more criticism to the company and even calls for Lajous' resignation.

In November a gasoline storage tank blaze outside Mexico City killed four people and sent flames hundred of yards (meters) into the air. Two workers were killed at another gasoline storage plant earlier this month in northern Mexico City.

The company's environmental record was also scarred last month when Greenpeace cruised down the Gulf of Mexico, accusing the state monopoly of leaving leaky platforms in the sea and killing fish. Lajous called the charges "exaggerations."
Local reporters raised many of the region's complaints to Pemex, from fishermen to the charges the company is disturbing the ecosystem.
"I'm not going to say the petroleum industry doesn't have environmental problems...but Pemex is planning to invest a considerable amount (to improve its record)," Lajous told reporters.
Cactus workers repeated what seemed to be a new motto: All accidents are preventable.

Damage to Cactus totaled $199.5 million in 1996, with the cost of lost production another $56 million, Pemex officials said. Two cryogenic plants at the complex, each with a production capacity of 500 million cfd, were almost completely destroyed.
